category: PSpice simulation, analyses, modelling & waveform analysis
description: The PSpice A/D and PSpice Advanced Analysis side of OrCAD: simulation profiles and analysis types, the netlist dot-command language and device model syntax, the Probe waveform viewer with its measurement and Performance Analysis machinery, the Stimulus and Model editors, behavioural modelling blocks, and the simulator options that control accuracy and convergence. Command-line switches listed here are the ones documented in the PSpice Reference Guide.

tools.name: New Simulation Profile
tools.description: Creates a named set of simulation settings inside the project: which analysis to run, which model and stimulus libraries are configured, which .prb display file to use and what simulator options apply. A design can hold many profiles (e.g. 'tran_startup', 'ac_loop', 'mc_worstcase') and the active one is chosen from the toolbar, so switching analyses never means re-typing settings.
tools.usage: PSpice > New Simulation Profile… (name it, optionally inherit from an existing profile)

parameters.name: Name
parameters.description: Profile name; also the base name of the generated .cir/.out/.dat files.

parameters.name: Inherit From
parameters.description: Copies an existing profile's settings as the starting point.

tools.example: PSpice > New Simulation Profile > name 'tran_1ms' > Analysis type: Time Domain (Transient), Run to time 1ms, Maximum step size 100n > Apply > OK.
tools.notes: Edit an existing one with PSpice > Edit Simulation Profile; the profile also owns the Configuration Files tab where .lib and .stl files are attached.

tools.name: Bias Point analysis
tools.description: Computes the DC operating point of the circuit with capacitors open and inductors shorted, and reports every node voltage, source current and the small-signal parameters of each semiconductor into the .out file. It runs automatically before AC and transient analyses, so a design that will not converge here will not simulate at all. Enable 'Include detailed bias point information for nonlinear controlled sources and semiconductors' to get the full device dump.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Analysis > Analysis type: Bias Point

parameters.name: Include detailed bias point information
parameters.description: Writes the .OP small-signal parameters (gm, gpi, ro, beta) of every semiconductor to the output file.

parameters.name: Perform Sensitivity analysis (.SENS)
parameters.description: Reports DC sensitivity of chosen outputs to every parameter.

parameters.name: Calculate small-signal DC gain (.TF)
parameters.description: Transfer function: gain plus input and output resistance between a source and an output variable.

tools.example: Analysis type: Bias Point; tick 'Calculate small-signal DC gain (.TF)', From Input source name: Vin, To Output Variable: V(out).
tools.notes: Bias point node voltages can also be displayed directly on the schematic with the V/I/W display toggles after a run.

tools.name: DC Sweep analysis
tools.description: Sweeps a voltage source, current source, global parameter, model parameter or temperature over a range and recomputes the bias point at each step, producing transfer curves such as a transistor's I-V family or a regulator's line regulation. A secondary sweep adds a nested variable, giving families of curves on one plot.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Analysis type: DC Sweep; choose sweep variable, sweep type (Linear, Logarithmic, Value list), start/end/increment

parameters.name: Sweep variable
parameters.description: Voltage source, Current source, Global parameter, Model parameter or Temperature.

parameters.name: Sweep type
parameters.description: Linear, Logarithmic (Decade/Octave) or an explicit Value list.

parameters.name: Secondary Sweep
parameters.description: Optional nested second variable producing a family of curves.

tools.example: Primary: Voltage source VCE, Linear, 0 to 5 V, 0.01 V. Secondary: Current source IB, Value list 10u 20u 30u 40u. Result: the transistor output characteristic family.
tools.notes: Generates the .DC card in the netlist. If it fails to converge, reduce the step size or raise ITL2.

tools.name: AC Sweep / Noise analysis
tools.description: Linearises the circuit about its bias point and sweeps frequency, giving gain, phase, impedance and, when noise is enabled, the output and equivalent input noise spectral densities with a per-device contribution breakdown in the .out file. It is the analysis for filter response, loop gain and amplifier bandwidth.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Analysis type: AC Sweep/Noise; set Linear or Logarithmic (Decade/Octave), Start/End Frequency, Points per decade

parameters.name: AC Sweep Type
parameters.description: Linear, or Logarithmic by Octave or Decade.

parameters.name: Points/Decade
parameters.description: Resolution of the sweep; 100/decade is typical for loop-gain plots.

parameters.name: Enable Noise / Output Voltage / I or V Source
parameters.description: Turns on .NOISE and names the output node and the input source for the equivalent-input-noise referral.

parameters.name: Interval
parameters.description: How often the per-device noise contribution table is printed to the .out file.

tools.example: AC Sweep, Logarithmic Decade, 10 Hz to 10 MHz, 100 points/decade; add a VDB marker on the output to plot gain in dB.
tools.notes: The stimulating source must have a non-zero AC magnitude (set the AC property, typically 1) or the response is identically zero.

tools.name: Time Domain (Transient) analysis
tools.description: Integrates the nonlinear circuit equations over time, the workhorse analysis for switching converters, oscillators, digital timing and start-up behaviour. Run-to time, the point where data recording starts and the maximum step size are the three settings that matter; the step ceiling must be small enough to resolve the fastest edge of interest or the waveform is aliased.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Analysis type: Time Domain (Transient); set Run to time, Start saving data after, Maximum step size

parameters.name: Run to time
parameters.description: Simulated stop time, e.g. 20ms.

parameters.name: Start saving data after
parameters.description: Skips recording the start-up transient to keep the .dat file small.

parameters.name: Maximum step size
parameters.description: Upper bound on the internal timestep; the main lever against aliased or ragged waveforms.

parameters.name: Skip initial transient bias point calculation (SKIPBP)
parameters.description: Starts from the .IC values instead of solving the operating point, used to kick-start oscillators.

parameters.name: Output File Options > Fourier
parameters.description: Adds .FOUR to compute harmonic amplitudes and THD of a named output.

tools.example: Run to time 20m, Start saving data after 10m, Maximum step size 1u; tick Fourier with Center Frequency 1k, Number of Harmonics 9, Output Variables V(out).
tools.notes: Transient convergence failures ('time step too small') usually mean an unrealistic discontinuity: add small series resistance/parasitics, give switches finite rise times, or relax RELTOL slightly.

tools.name: Parametric Sweep
tools.description: Repeats the chosen primary analysis while stepping a global parameter, model parameter, component value, source or temperature, producing a family of curves in one data file. It is how component tolerance sensitivity, compensation network tuning and load sweeps are explored. The swept value is defined with a PARAM block on the schematic and referenced as {name}.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Options > Parametric Sweep; choose sweep variable and Linear / Logarithmic / Value list

parameters.name: Global parameter
parameters.description: A name declared in a PARAM part, referenced in a component value as {Rload}.

parameters.name: Model parameter
parameters.description: Steps a named parameter of a named .MODEL.

parameters.name: Value list
parameters.description: Explicit set of values, the usual choice for E12 component series.

tools.example: Add a PARAM part with Rload = 10. Set R1 Value to {Rload}. Options > Parametric Sweep > Global parameter Rload > Value list 1 10 100 1k. Probe then offers a section per value.
tools.notes: Emits .STEP in the netlist. Combine with Probe's Performance Analysis to plot a measured quantity (e.g. bandwidth) against the swept parameter.

tools.name: Temperature Sweep
tools.description: Re-runs the analysis at a list of temperatures, applying every model's temperature coefficients (TC1/TC2 on resistors, IS and BF drift in semiconductors) so that drift and worst-case hot/cold behaviour can be seen directly. Available as a simulation option alongside the primary analysis.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Options > Temperature (Sweep); enter a value list or a range
tools.example: Options > Temperature (Sweep) > Repeat the simulation for each of the temperatures: -40 25 85 125.
tools.notes: Emits .TEMP. Component temperature coefficients must actually be set (TC1/TC2 properties) or the sweep changes nothing for passives.

tools.name: Monte Carlo analysis
tools.description: Runs the analysis many times with component values randomly perturbed inside their declared tolerances, producing a statistical picture of yield. Tolerances come from DEV (per-device random) and LOT (correlated across devices sharing a model) qualifiers on .MODEL parameters. Collating functions (YMAX, MAX, MIN, RISE_EDGE, FALL_EDGE) summarise each run so a histogram of the metric can be built.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Options > Monte Carlo/Worst Case > Monte Carlo; set Number of runs, Output variable and Collating function

parameters.name: Number of runs
parameters.description: How many randomised runs; a few hundred is typical for a yield estimate.

parameters.name: Use distribution
parameters.description: Uniform, Gaussian or a user-defined .DISTRIBUTION.

parameters.name: Random number seed
parameters.description: Fixing the seed makes a run reproducible.

parameters.name: Save data from
parameters.description: All / First n / Every nth / Runs list — keeps the .dat file manageable.

parameters.name: MC Load/Save
parameters.description: Saves the generated parameter sets so an interesting run can be reproduced exactly.

tools.example:
.MODEL Rmod RES(R=1 DEV=1% LOT=0.5%)
— then Options > Monte Carlo, 200 runs, Gaussian, output V(out), collating function YMAX.
tools.notes: Emits .MC. Passive parts must reference a tolerance-bearing .MODEL (Rbreak/Cbreak/Lbreak) — a plain numeric value has no tolerance to randomise.

tools.name: Worst-Case (Sensitivity) analysis
tools.description: First perturbs each toleranced parameter one at a time to find the direction in which it pushes the chosen output, then performs a single run with every parameter set to its worst extreme in that direction. It gives the absolute corner rather than a statistical spread, which is what specification limits require.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Options > Monte Carlo/Worst Case > Worst-case/Sensitivity; set Output variable, Collating function and Vary device/lot

parameters.name: Vary
parameters.description: Devices only (DEV), lot only (LOT), or both.

parameters.name: Direction
parameters.description: HI or LOW — which extreme of the output is the worst case.

parameters.name: Collating function
parameters.description: YMAX, MAX, MIN, RISE_EDGE or FALL_EDGE applied to the output waveform.

tools.example: Options > Monte Carlo/Worst Case > Worst-case/Sensitivity, Output variable V(out), function MAX, Vary both DEV and LOT, Direction HI.
tools.notes: Emits .WCASE. The sensitivity phase assumes monotonic behaviour; for strongly nonlinear circuits Monte Carlo is the safer answer.

tools.name: Sensitivity analysis (.SENS)
tools.description: DC sensitivity: reports how much each device parameter influences a chosen set of DC output variables, expressed both per unit and per percent. Use it to find which handful of components actually control an output before spending money on tighter tolerances.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Analysis type: Bias Point > tick 'Perform Sensitivity analysis (.SENS)', list the output variables
tools.example: Bias Point > Perform Sensitivity analysis, Output variable(s): V(out) — the .out file then ranks every resistor's contribution.
tools.notes: Results go to the .out text file, not to Probe.

tools.name: Transfer Function (.TF)
tools.description: Computes the small-signal DC transfer function between a named input source and a named output variable, plus the small-signal input resistance at the source and output resistance at the output node. It is the quick way to get a DC gain and impedance summary without drawing a sweep.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Analysis type: Bias Point > tick 'Calculate small-signal DC gain (.TF)'
tools.example: From Input source name: Vin ; To Output Variable: V(out). The .out file reports V(out)/Vin, INPUT RESISTANCE AT Vin and OUTPUT RESISTANCE AT V(out).

tools.name: Optimizer (PSpice Advanced Analysis)
tools.description: Adjusts chosen component values to meet stated design goals — bandwidth, ripple, efficiency, overshoot — within declared parameter ranges, using modified least-squares-quadratic, random and discrete engines. The discrete engine then snaps the result onto real E-series values. Part of PSpice Advanced Analysis, launched from the PSpice menu with the design's simulation profile.
tools.usage: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Optimizer; declare parameters with ranges and specifications with goals

parameters.name: Parameters
parameters.description: Editable component values with min/max limits, taken from parts with tolerance-bearing models.

parameters.name: Specifications
parameters.description: Measurement expressions (e.g. Bandwidth(V(out),3)) with target values and weights.

parameters.name: Engine
parameters.description: LSQ (modified least-squares quadratic), Random, or Discrete for standard component values.

tools.example: Specification: Bandwidth(V(out),3) target 100k; Parameters: R2 (1k..100k), C1 (1n..100n); run the LSQ engine then the Discrete engine to land on E24 values.
tools.notes: Requires an Advanced Analysis licence; the base PSpice A/D product does not include it.

tools.name: Smoke analysis (PSpice Advanced Analysis)
tools.description: Stress/reliability analysis: checks every component against its safe operating limits — power dissipation, junction temperature, breakdown voltage, peak current, dV/dt — using the smoke parameters attached to the part, and reports the percentage of maximum for each. Derating tables (standard, MIL, user-defined) can be applied so parts are judged against a derated rather than absolute limit.
tools.usage: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Smoke; run after a transient or DC analysis

parameters.name: Derating file
parameters.description: Applies a derating profile so limits are scaled (e.g. 80 % of rated power).

parameters.name: Max Derating / % Max
parameters.description: Reported stress against the derated limit; entries over 100 % are flagged.

tools.example: Run a 20 ms transient, then PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Smoke; review the table for any RV (voltage), PDM (power) or TB (junction temperature) entry above 100 %.
tools.notes: Only parts that carry smoke parameters are checked; generic breakout parts report nothing.

tools.name: Probe waveform viewer
tools.description: The plotting environment that opens with (or after) a simulation and reads the .dat waveform file. It supports multiple plots and Y axes, log/linear axes, sectioned data from parametric and Monte Carlo runs, cursors with measurement readouts, arithmetic on traces, FFT, and Performance Analysis. Probe's own actions can be recorded to a command file and replayed, which is how simulation post-processing is automated.
tools.usage: Opens automatically on PSpice > Run, or open a .dat file directly in the PSpice A/D application
tools.example: PSpice > Run; in Probe use Trace > Add Trace, enter `V(out)` and `V(out)/V(in)`, then Plot > Add Y Axis for the ratio.
tools.notes: Probe reads only what the netlist saved: a .PROBE with an explicit list, or a marker on the schematic, limits the stored variables.

tools.name: Add Trace
tools.description: Adds one or more waveforms to the active plot. The dialog lists every saved simulation output variable and a palette of functions, and accepts arithmetic expressions combining them, so derived quantities (instantaneous power, differential voltage, efficiency) are plotted without re-simulating.
tools.usage: Trace > Add Trace… (Insert key); enter a trace expression

parameters.name: Simulation Output Variables
parameters.description: Voltages V(node), currents I(device), digital signals, device power W(device).

parameters.name: Functions or Macros
parameters.description: ABS, AVG, AVGX, D (derivative), S (integral), RMS, SQRT, LOG, DB, M (magnitude), P (phase), R/IMG, MIN, MAX.

parameters.name: Analog / Digital / Voltages / Currents / Power filters
parameters.description: Checkboxes that shorten the variable list.

tools.example: Trace > Add Trace: `V(out)` then `V(D:1)-V(D:2)` then `AVG(W(M1))` for average MOSFET dissipation.

tools.name: Cursors and cursor search commands
tools.description: Two cursors that snap to trace data points and display X, Y and the difference between them in the readout box. Search Commands drive a cursor to a characteristic point automatically — a peak, a trough, a level crossing, a slope — which makes measurements repeatable and scriptable inside a Probe command file.
tools.usage: Trace > Cursor > Display (toggle); Trace > Cursor > Search Commands…, Peak, Trough, Next/Previous, Max, Min

parameters.name: Search Commands
parameters.description: Expressions such as `search forward level(3)` or `search forward max` to position the cursor.

parameters.name: Mark Label
parameters.description: Pins the current cursor reading onto the plot as an annotation.

tools.example: Trace > Cursor > Display, then Search Commands: `sfle(2.5)!1` to place cursor 1 at the first forward crossing of 2.5 V.
tools.notes: Cursor movements are deliberately NOT recorded into command files, so automate them with Search Commands rather than mouse actions.

tools.name: Evaluate Measurement / measurement functions
tools.description: Applies a built-in or user-defined measurement to a trace and prints the numeric result: Max, Min, Peak-to-peak, Bandwidth, Bandwidth_Bandpass_3dB, Rise_Time, Fall_Time, Overshoot, Period, Duty_Cycle, Falltime_NoOvershoot, Cutoff_Lowpass_3dB, GainMargin, PhaseMargin, CenterFrequency, SettlingTime, YatX, XatNthY and more. It replaces manual cursor reading and feeds Performance Analysis.
tools.usage: Trace > Evaluate Measurement…, pick a measurement and its trace/arguments

parameters.name: Measurement
parameters.description: The goal function to apply, e.g. Bandwidth(1,db_level).

parameters.name: Arguments
parameters.description: Trace expression plus any numeric arguments such as the dB level or threshold.

tools.example: Trace > Evaluate Measurement > `Bandwidth(V(out),3)` returns the -3 dB bandwidth; `Rise_Time(V(out))` returns the 10-90 % rise time.
tools.notes: Measurements are defined as goal functions in .prb files; custom ones are added with Trace > Goal Functions and travel with the -p file.

tools.name: Performance Analysis
tools.description: Plots a measurement taken from each section of a multi-run simulation against the variable that changed, turning a parametric, temperature or Monte Carlo sweep into a single meaningful curve or histogram — for example bandwidth versus load resistance, or a histogram of output ripple across 200 Monte Carlo runs. It is the payoff for running swept analyses.
tools.usage: Trace > Performance Analysis… > Wizard, then choose a goal function and its trace
tools.example: After a parametric sweep of Rload, Trace > Performance Analysis > Wizard > goal function Bandwidth, trace V(out), level 3 — Probe plots bandwidth versus Rload.
tools.notes: For Monte Carlo data the same command produces a histogram with mean, sigma and yield percentages.

tools.name: Fourier / FFT in Probe
tools.description: Switches the X axis of a transient plot to frequency and displays the discrete Fourier transform of the displayed traces, used for harmonic content, EMI spectra and noise floor inspection. The separate .FOUR netlist command computes tabulated harmonic amplitudes, phases and THD into the .out file instead.
tools.usage: Trace > Fourier (toggle) on a transient plot; or Simulation Settings > Output File Options > Perform Fourier Analysis (.FOUR)
tools.example: Run a 20 ms transient of a class-D output, add V(spk), then Trace > Fourier and set the X axis range to 0-100 kHz.
tools.notes: FFT resolution is set by the transient run length and the maximum step size; short runs give coarse bins and spectral leakage.

tools.name: Markers (voltage, current, power, differential)
tools.description: Symbols placed on the schematic that tell PSpice which quantities to save and tell Probe which traces to display automatically after a run. Types include Voltage Level, Voltage Differential (a pair), Current Into Pin, Power Dissipation, plus advanced markers for dB magnitude, phase, real and imaginary parts.
tools.usage: PSpice > Markers > Voltage Level / Current Into Pin / Power Dissipation / Advanced > (dB Magnitude of Voltage, Phase of Voltage, …)
tools.example: PSpice > Markers > Advanced > dB Magnitude of Voltage, click the filter output; run the AC sweep and Probe opens with the Bode magnitude already plotted.
tools.notes: Markers also restrict what is written to the .dat file when 'Save data in the CSDF format'/limited .PROBE is used, which keeps large sweeps manageable.

tools.name: Stimulus Editor
tools.description: A graphical editor for source waveforms that writes a .stl stimulus file. It supports the analog source shapes — PWL (piecewise linear), PULSE, SIN, EXP, SFFM — and digital stimuli (clocks, patterns, buses), showing the resulting waveform as it is edited. Sources on the schematic (VSTIM/ISTIM, DigStim) reference stimuli by name.
tools.usage: PSpice > Edit Stimulus (with a stimulus source selected), or double-click a VSTIM part

parameters.name: PWL
parameters.description: Arbitrary piecewise-linear time/value pairs, optionally repeating.

parameters.name: PULSE
parameters.description: V1 V2 TD TR TF PW PER — the standard rectangular source.

parameters.name: SIN
parameters.description: VOFF VAMPL FREQ TD DF PHASE — damped sinusoid.

parameters.name: EXP
parameters.description: V1 V2 TD1 TC1 TD2 TC2 — exponential rise and fall.

parameters.name: SFFM
parameters.description: VOFF VAMPL FC MDI FS — single-frequency FM for intermodulation tests.

tools.example: Select the VSTIM source, PSpice > Edit Stimulus, choose PULSE, V1=0 V2=3.3 TD=0 TR=2n TF=2n PW=100n PER=200n, save as clk in stim.stl.
tools.notes: The .stl file must be listed on the simulation profile's Configuration Files > Stimulus tab or the source resolves to nothing.

tools.name: Model Editor
tools.description: Creates and edits PSpice device models. It can extract model parameters from datasheet curves for diodes, BJTs, MOSFETs, IGBTs, op-amps, magnetic cores and transformers by fitting to entered characteristics, or edit the raw .MODEL/.SUBCKT text directly. Output is written into a .lib model library that the simulation profile then references.
tools.usage: PSpice > Model Editor (or right-click a part > Edit PSpice Model)

parameters.name: Model type
parameters.description: Diode, Bipolar Transistor, MOSFET, IGBT, JFET, Operational Amplifier, Magnetic Core, Voltage Comparator, Voltage Regulator/Reference.

parameters.name: Extract from curves
parameters.description: Enter datasheet points (forward current, capacitance, reverse recovery) and let the fitter derive the parameters.

parameters.name: Save As Library
parameters.description: Writes a .lib that must be added to the profile's Configuration Files.

tools.example: PSpice > Model Editor > File > New > Diode, enter the forward I-V points and Cj from the datasheet, Extract Parameters, File > Save As mydiodes.lib.
tools.notes: Editing a part's model from the schematic creates a design-local copy in a <design>.lib; that copy shadows the shipped library, which surprises people who then edit the shipped file with no effect.

tools.name: Model Import Wizard / PSpice Modeling Application
tools.description: Brings vendor-supplied SPICE models into a usable Capture part: the wizard reads a .lib or .txt containing .SUBCKT/.MODEL definitions, matches the terminals to a symbol (existing or newly generated) and registers the model in the project's configuration. The PSpice Modeling Application in OrCAD X extends this with template-based model creation for common device classes.
tools.usage: PSpice > Model Import Wizard… ; or the Modeling Application from the PSpice menu (OrCAD X)
tools.example: Download the vendor .lib, PSpice > Model Import Wizard, point at the file, select the .SUBCKT, choose 'Create a new symbol', map pins, finish — the part is now placeable and simulatable.
tools.notes: Encrypted vendor models still simulate but cannot be inspected or edited; some require a matching PSpice version.

tools.name: Analog Behavioral Modeling (ABM) blocks
tools.description: Parts from the ABM library that implement a mathematical relationship rather than physical devices, used to model control loops, sensors, transfer functions and idealised blocks. The family covers arbitrary expressions (ABM, ABM1..ABM3, ABM/I variants), controlled sources with expressions (EVALUE, GVALUE), lookup tables (ETABLE, GTABLE), s-domain transfer functions (ELAPLACE, GLAPLACE), frequency-response tables (EFREQ, GFREQ), multipliers, summers, integrators, differentiators, limiters and math functions.
tools.usage: Place > Part from the ABM library; edit the EXPR / TABLE / XFORM property

parameters.name: EVALUE / GVALUE
parameters.description: Voltage- or current-output source whose value is an arbitrary expression of node voltages and currents.

parameters.name: ETABLE / GTABLE
parameters.description: Piecewise-linear transfer characteristic given as (input, output) pairs.

parameters.name: ELAPLACE / GLAPLACE
parameters.description: Laplace-domain transfer function in s, e.g. `1/(1+0.001*s)`.

parameters.name: EFREQ / GFREQ
parameters.description: Response given as a table of frequency, magnitude(dB) and phase points.

tools.example: Place an EVALUE part and set EXPR to `V(%IN+, %IN-)*V(%IN+, %IN-)` for a squaring block, or an ELAPLACE with XFORM `1/(1+s/6283)` for a 1 kHz pole.
tools.notes: Laplace and frequency-table blocks are exact in AC analysis but are approximated by convolution in transient runs, which can be slow and can ring if the response is not band-limited.

tools.name: Digital and mixed-signal simulation
tools.description: PSpice A/D simulates digital primitives and behavioural digital blocks event-driven alongside the analog solver, inserting analog/digital interface subcircuits automatically at the boundary. Digital parts carry min/typ/max propagation delays, so timing can be simulated at any corner, and timing violations (setup, hold, width) are reported as warnings or persistent errors.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Options > Gate-level Simulation: Timing Mode (Min/Typ/Max/Worst-case Min-Max), Suppress simulation error messages

parameters.name: Timing Mode
parameters.description: Minimum, Typical, Maximum, or Worst-case (min/max) ambiguity propagation.

parameters.name: Default A/D Interface Digital Power/Ground
parameters.description: Which supply the automatically inserted interface subcircuits use, e.g. $G_DPWR/$G_DGND.

parameters.name: Initialize all flip-flops to
parameters.description: X, 0 or 1 at time zero.

tools.example: Options > Gate-level Simulation > Timing Mode: Worst-case (min/max); run the transient and look for hazard/ambiguity regions drawn on the digital traces in Probe.
tools.notes: Analog nodes driving digital inputs need a defined interface supply; missing DPWR/DGND is the usual cause of 'unable to determine interface' errors.

tools.name: .MODEL
tools.description: Netlist card that defines a named set of device parameters shared by many instances — resistors with tolerance and temperature coefficients, diodes, BJTs, MOSFETs, switches and more. It is also where Monte Carlo tolerances live, as DEV and LOT qualifiers on individual parameters.
tools.usage: .MODEL <name> <type>([parameter=value]* [DEV=x%] [LOT=y%])

parameters.name: <type>
parameters.description: RES, CAP, IND, D, NPN, PNP, NMOS, PMOS, NJF, PJF, VSWITCH, ISWITCH, CORE, GASFET …

parameters.name: DEV
parameters.description: Independent random tolerance applied per device instance.

parameters.name: LOT
parameters.description: Correlated tolerance applied identically to every device sharing the model.

tools.example:
.MODEL Rtol RES(R=1 DEV=1% LOT=0.5% TC1=100u)
R1 in out RESISTOR Rtol 10k

tools.name: .SUBCKT / .ENDS
tools.description: Defines a reusable subcircuit with named terminals and optional parameters, instantiated in the netlist with an X card. Vendor IC models are almost always distributed as .SUBCKT blocks, and hierarchical Capture blocks netlist into the same construct.
tools.usage:
.SUBCKT <name> <node>* [PARAMS: <param>=<value>*]
… body …
.ENDS [name]

tools.name: .LIB / .INC
tools.description: Brings external model text into the simulation. `.LIB` attaches an indexed model library and pulls in only the models actually referenced (fast, the normal choice, and what the profile's Configuration Files tab generates); `.INC` textually inserts an entire file, which is right for a handful of definitions or a shared parameter block.
tools.usage: .LIB "<file.lib>"   |   .INC "<file>"
tools.example:
.LIB "nom.lib"
.LIB "C:/models/vendor_opamps.lib"
.INC "project_params.inc"
tools.notes: nom.lib is the master library that includes the shipped model set; a profile missing it is the classic cause of 'Model X not found'.

tools.name: .PARAM / .FUNC / .STEP
tools.description: Parameterisation of a netlist. `.PARAM` declares named values usable in any expression as {name}; `.FUNC` defines a reusable inline function; `.STEP` repeats the analysis across a list or range of a parameter, model parameter, source, component or temperature (the netlist form of the Parametric Sweep option).

tools.name: .IC / .NODESET
tools.description: Convergence and start-up aids. `.NODESET` supplies an initial guess for the DC solution that the solver is free to move away from, used to steer bistable circuits to the intended state; `.IC` forces node voltages for the transient analysis and holds them during the bias point, used to set starting conditions on capacitors and to kick oscillators.
tools.usage: .IC V(node)=value …   |   .NODESET V(node)=value …
tools.example:
.NODESET V(q)=0 V(qbar)=5
.IC V(tank)=0.1
tools.notes: Combine `.IC` with the transient 'Skip initial transient bias point calculation' (SKIPBP) option to start an oscillator without a converged operating point.

tools.name: .OPTIONS
tools.description: Sets simulator accuracy, iteration and reporting controls. The convergence-relevant ones are RELTOL (relative tolerance on voltages and currents), VNTOL/ABSTOL (absolute voltage and current floors), GMIN (minimum conductance added across every branch), ITL1/ITL2/ITL4 (iteration limits for bias point, DC sweep and transient timepoints) and STEPGMIN/ITL6 (Gmin stepping). NUMDGT, NOECHO, NOBIAS and NOPAGE control the output file.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS <name>=<value> … ; or Simulation Settings > Options > Analog Simulation

parameters.name: RELTOL
parameters.description: Relative accuracy, default 0.001. Raising to 0.01 often fixes stubborn transient convergence at the cost of accuracy.

parameters.name: ABSTOL / VNTOL
parameters.description: Absolute current (default 1pA) and voltage (default 1uV) tolerances; raise them for high-power circuits, lower for nanoamp designs.

parameters.name: GMIN
parameters.description: Minimum conductance across every branch, default 1e-12; raising it helps floating-node convergence.

parameters.name: ITL1 / ITL2 / ITL4
parameters.description: Iteration limits for the bias point, DC sweep and each transient timepoint.

parameters.name: STEPGMIN
parameters.description: Enables Gmin stepping, an automatic continuation method for hard operating points.

tools.example: .OPTIONS RELTOL=0.01 ABSTOL=1u VNTOL=1m ITL4=100 STEPGMIN
tools.notes: Change one option at a time and re-check results: loosening tolerances can silently turn a wrong answer into a converged wrong answer.

tools.name: .PROBE / .PRINT / .PLOT
tools.description: Control what a run records. `.PROBE` writes the binary waveform data file read by the Probe viewer — with no arguments it saves everything, with a variable list it saves only those, which matters for long sweeps. `.PRINT` writes tabulated values into the .out text file and `.PLOT` writes a line-printer-style plot; both are the machine-readable route for external post-processing.
tools.usage:
.PROBE [/CSDF] [output variables]
.PRINT <analysis> <output variables>
.PLOT <analysis> <output variables>
tools.example:
.PROBE V(out) I(L1) W(M1)
.PRINT TRAN V(out) V(in)
.PRINT AC VDB(out) VP(out)
tools.notes: `.PROBE/CSDF` writes the portable text CSDF format instead of the binary .dat when the file must cross machines or be parsed by another program.

tools.name: .FOUR
tools.description: Performs a Fourier decomposition of a transient output over the last full period of the run, printing DC component, harmonic amplitudes and phases, normalised values and total harmonic distortion into the .out file. It is the numeric counterpart to Probe's FFT display.
tools.usage: .FOUR <fundamental frequency> [number of harmonics] <output variables>
tools.example:
.TRAN 1u 20m 10m
.FOUR 1k 9 V(out)
tools.notes: Accuracy depends on having an integer number of fundamental periods in the analysed window and a small enough maximum step size.

tools.name: Device card syntax (R C L D Q M J X V I E F G H K T S W)
tools.description: The one-line element statements that make up a PSpice netlist. The first letter selects the device: R/C/L passives, K coupling between inductors, D diode, Q bipolar, M MOSFET, J JFET, Z IGBT, T/O transmission lines, S/W voltage- and current-controlled switches, V/I independent sources, E/G/F/H the four linear controlled sources, and X a subcircuit instance. Node order is fixed per device type and is the usual source of hand-netlisting errors.
tools.usage: <name> <node+> <node-> [model] <value/parameters>
tools.example:
R1 in out 10k
C1 out 0 100n IC=0
L1 sw out 10u
K1 L1 L2 0.98
D1 a k DIODE_MODEL
Q1 c b e Q2N3904
M1 d g s b IRF540 L=1u W=1m
V1 in 0 DC 5 AC 1 PULSE(0 5 0 1n 1n 1u 2u)
E1 out 0 VALUE={2*V(in)}
X1 in out RC_LP
tools.notes: For Q and M the substrate/bulk node is optional in some variants and mandatory in others; always check the model's expected terminal order.

tools.name: pspice -r (run a simulation from the command line)
tools.description: Runs PSpice headless on one or more input files. Without `-r` the files are merely opened; with it the simulation executes. Combine with `-o`, `-d` and `-e` to name the output and waveform files and exit afterwards, which is the standard CI/build integration for a simulation regression suite.
tools.usage: pspice [-r] [-o <output file>] [-d <data file>] [-e] [-t <temp dir>] <input file(s)>

parameters.name: -r
parameters.description: Run the specified simulation files (otherwise they are only opened).

parameters.name: -o <output file>
parameters.description: Text output file; defaults to the input name with .out.

parameters.name: -d <data file>
parameters.description: Waveform data file; defaults to the input name with .dat.

parameters.name: -e
parameters.description: Exit PSpice once every specified file has been simulated (replaces the old -wONLY).

parameters.name: -i <ini file>
parameters.description: Use an alternate initialisation file instead of pspice.ini.

parameters.name: -t <dir>
parameters.description: Directory for temporary files.

parameters.name: -bf / -bn / -bs
parameters.description: Waveform file buffer flush interval (minutes), buffer count and buffer size factor.

tools.example:
pspice -r amp.cir -o amp.out -d amp.dat -e
# then parse amp.out for "Total Harmonic Distortion" or read amp.dat with a Probe command file
tools.notes: Options accept either `-` or `/` as the separator and are case-insensitive; the order does not matter and they may be run together without spaces.

tools.name: Probe command files (-c / -l)
tools.description: Automates the waveform viewer. `-c` runs a command file of Probe menu actions until it ends or PSpice stops; `-l` records the session's commands into a log file that is itself a valid command file. Inside Probe the same pair is File > Run Commands and File > Log Commands. Commands are menu names one per line, `*` starts a comment, PAUSE waits for a keypress, and @CR/@UP/@DWN/@LEFT/@RIGHT/@ESC stand in for keystrokes.
tools.usage: pspice -c <file.cmd> -l <file.log> <input file>
tools.example:
* example.cmd — draw a trace, wait, exit
Trace Add
v(out2)
Pause
File Exit
tools.notes: Default extensions are assumed, so `-c makeplot` and `-c makeplot.cmd` are equivalent. PROBECMD and STMEDCMD lines in pspice.ini set a command file for every session.

tools.name: pspice.ini / PSPICECMDLINE
tools.description: PSpice's initialisation file. Editing the PSPICECMDLINE entry embeds command-line options that take effect for every subsequent start of PSpice A/D, and PRBFILE names the global .prb display/goal-function file. PROBECMD and STMEDCMD set default command files for Probe and the Stimulus Editor.
tools.usage: [PSPICE] section of pspice.ini: PSPICECMDLINE=-c makeplot.cmd -p newamp.prb
tools.example:
PSPICECMDLINE=-c makeplot -p newamp
PRBFILE=pspice.prb
tools.notes: Options can be separated by spaces or run together; `-cmakeplot.cmd-pnewamp.prb` and the spaced form are equivalent.

tools.name: Simulation output file (.out) inspection
tools.description: The text transcript of a run: the echoed netlist, the model and library resolution, the bias point solution, .OP device parameters, .PRINT/.PLOT tables, .FOUR and .SENS results, warnings, and the convergence and timing summary at the end. For automated regressions it is the file to parse, because every numeric result requested with .PRINT, .FOUR, .TF or .SENS lands here as plain text.
tools.usage: PSpice > View > Output File; or read <profile>.out directly
tools.example: grep -A5 "TOTAL HARMONIC DISTORTION" amp.out
tools.notes: Convergence failures name the offending node and time point here — always read the .out before assuming the model is wrong.

tools.name: Convergence troubleshooting workflow
tools.description: The standard sequence when a simulation will not converge. Bias point failures: check for floating nodes and missing DC paths to ground, add .NODESET guesses, enable STEPGMIN/Gmin stepping, raise GMIN, increase ITL1. Transient 'time step too small': add realistic parasitics (ESR, lead inductance, snubbers), give ideal switches and sources finite rise/fall times, reduce the maximum step size, relax RELTOL to 0.01 and raise ABSTOL/VNTOL to match the circuit's real current and voltage scales, then increase ITL4.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Options > Analog Simulation (GMIN, RELTOL, ABSTOL, VNTOL, ITL1/2/4, STEPGMIN)
tools.example:
1. Read the .out file for the failing node and time.
2. Add `.OPTIONS STEPGMIN` and re-run the bias point.
3. If transient still fails: `.OPTIONS RELTOL=0.01 ABSTOL=1u VNTOL=1m ITL4=100` and set a maximum step size of about 1/100 of the fastest edge.
tools.notes: Every relaxation trades accuracy for convergence. Once the run completes, tighten the options back one at a time and confirm the answer does not move.

tools.name: PSpice / MATLAB-Simulink co-simulation (SLPS)
tools.description: The PSpice Systems Option couples PSpice to MathWorks Simulink so that an electrical circuit solved by PSpice appears as a block inside a Simulink model and mechanical, thermal, hydraulic and control-system blocks solve in the same run. Use it for motor drives, power-electronics-plus-control loops and ECU-level system validation where neither tool alone covers the whole system.
tools.usage: Install the PSpice Systems Option; place the SLPS block in Simulink and point it at the PSpice design
tools.example:
1. Create the PSpice design with the interface ports.
2. In Simulink, add the SLPS block and browse to the .dsn/.cir.
3. Wire Simulink signals to the mapped PSpice ports and run the model.
tools.notes: Requires matching supported releases of MATLAB and OrCAD; the interface is configured through dialogs rather than a documented text API.
